abstract: Abstract The cage‐amine molecules nona(ethylene)hexamine and dodeka(ethylene)octamine, have been prepared by coupling 1,4,7‐triazacyclononane (tacn) or 1,4,7,10‐tetraazacyclododecane (cyclen) to the corresponding α‐chloroacetamide derivatives of these macrocycles. The formed tri‐ or tetra‐amide cryptands were then reduced to the corresponding hexamine and octamine with borane. In all cases, the amide and amine cryptands were isolated as protonated ammonium salts, with the proton oriented to the inside of the cage molecules (i.e., endohedral). Deprotonation studies on the hexamine and octamine showed the encapsulated protons are highly inert, with no evidence of deprotonation or deuterium exchange. Detailed theoretical studies predict very high proton affinity and basicity of 1118.7 and 1086.7 kJ mol −1 , respectively, for dodeka(ethylene)octamine, and 1108.3 and 1083.7 kJ mol −1 , respectively, for nona(ethylene)hexamine, placing them among the strongest amine bases ever prepared and firmly within the realm of “superbases”.

Conclusion
The protonated cage‐amines nona(ethylene)hexamine
10H
⋅Cl and dodeka(ethylene)octamine
5H
⋅Cl have been successfully prepared for the first time. For both
10H
.
Cl and
5H
.
Cl the encapsulated N ─
H
proton is highly inert and neither deprotonation nor deuterium exchange occurred in the presence of NaOD, DBU, or NaH. The strong base CH
3
Li did not result in removal of the encapsulated ammonium proton but rather C─H deprotonation of a methylene group in a Hoffman‐type elimination process and ring opening of the cage molecules. Theoretical studies predict very high proton affinities and basicities of 1118.7 and 1086.7 kJ mol
−1
, respectively, for
5
and 1108.3 and 1083.7 kJ mol
−1
, respectively, for
10
placing them among the strongest amine bases ever prepared.
[
3
,
5
]
However, as has been previously demonstrated for related compounds, e.g., the protonated forms of
3
and
4
(Figure
1
),
[
7
,
27
]
the very high proton affinities of
10
and
5
are unlikely to account for the inertness of these molecules alone. The inability to deprotonate these compounds can also be ascribed to the complete steric inaccessibility of the encapsulated proton to external reactants. In this way, these compounds can accurately be described as “proton traps” (a term coined to describe the inertness of protonated adamanzanes)
[
1c
]
and their lack of reactivity can be significantly ascribed as a kinetic phenomenon resulting from the complete encapsulation of the ammonium proton.
